meta.title: Who really said "People say nothing is impossible, but I do nothing every day"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — A. A. Milne never wrote this. It’s an anonymous joke printed in 1906, twenty years before Winnie-the-Pooh. Quote Investigator traced the real origin.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'People say nothing is impossible, but I do nothing every day'?
meta.ogDescription: Not A. A. Milne. This quip appeared in a 1906 humor almanac, two decades before Winnie-the-Pooh. It’s an anonymous joke, later pinned on Pooh.

answer.label: Not A. A. Milne — an anonymous joke
answer.sourceLine: This is a wandering anonymous quip, not a line from A. A. Milne. Quote Investigator ↗ traced it to a 1906 humor almanac — two decades before the first Winnie-the-Pooh book (1926) — and found no substantive evidence Milne ever used the expression. The wording drifted over the years before being pinned on Pooh in the internet era.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Foolish Almanak For Anuthur Year
1906, John W. Luce & Co., Boston (as by “Theodor Rosyfelt”)
“It is said that nothing is impossible; but there are lots of people doing nothing every day.”

source.excerpt: It is said that nothing is impossible; but there are lots of people doing nothing every day.
trail: 1906: The quip appears in a humor almanac as “It is said that nothing is impossible; but there are lots of people doing nothing every day,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
1968: Evan Esar reprinted a version, still unattributed, in 20,000 Quips and Quotes — documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
Modern era: Quote sites such as Goodreads ↗ pin it on “A.A. Milne, Winnie-the-Pooh,” a book that does not contain the line.
source.excerptNote: The 1906 form of the joke, per Quote Investigator ↗. The modern “People say nothing is impossible, but I do nothing every day” is a later, tightened paraphrase.
source.rightsNote: The earliest documented form was printed in 1906 (The Foolish Almanak For Anuthur Year), well before 1931, so that text is in the public domain in the United States. The exact modern wording is an anonymous paraphrase with no identifiable rights holder.

author.name: A. A. Milne
author.heading: The name it’s pinned on
author.bio: Alan Alexander Milne was an English playwright, novelist and poet best known for the Winnie-the-Pooh stories (1926–1928), written for his son Christopher Robin. His gentle, whimsical reputation makes him a frequent target for feel-good misquotes — this joke among them — that appear nowhere in his actual writing.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Pooh
misattribution.intro: A. A. Milne is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for feel-good misquotes, and this clever one-liner is a textbook case: an old anonymous joke retrofitted onto Winnie-the-Pooh long after the fact.

items.why: The line does not appear in The Complete Tales of Winnie-the-Pooh, and the joke predates the 1926 Pooh stories by twenty years. Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence Milne used the expression.
A 1997 Associated Press piece linked a form of the gag to Mad’s Alfred E. Neuman, but that too postdates the 1906 printing, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The real origin is an anonymous joke printed in a 1906 humor almanac; it was pinned on Milne only in the internet era, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Pooh
lead: Winnie-the-Pooh has become shorthand for gentle, paradoxical wisdom, so a witty line about the virtue (or vice) of “doing nothing” feels like something Pooh would say — which is exactly why it drifts to Milne. The pull is thematic, not textual.

In reality the joke is a pun on two senses of “nothing”: the motivational cliché that nothing is impossible, undercut by the deadpan admission that plenty of people accomplish nothing daily. That structure is a stock gag, printed and reprinted anonymously for over a century.
context.pull: An old anonymous pun, dressed up in a Pooh costume.
